title: Panna Cotta
subtitle: Silky set cream dessert from Piedmont
excerpt: Panna cotta is set cream at its simplest -- sweetened, flavoured, and chilled until it holds its shape but trembles when tipped onto a plate. It takes about ten minutes to make and the fridge does the rest. Serve with macerated berries or a sharp fruit sauce to cut through the richness.
sourceNotes: Panna cotta comes from Piedmont in north-west Italy, where rich dairy is central to the cooking. The name simply means 'cooked cream'. It has been served in Italian restaurants worldwide since the 1980s.

content.text: Do not let the cream boil after the gelatine goes in. High heat will stop the gelatine setting properly.

items.prepNote: use 3 gelatine leaves, soaked in cold water -- or 1 tsp agar agar for vegetarian version
use 1 tsp vanilla extract or seeds from 1 vanilla pod
serve with macerated berries or a simple strawberry sauce

content.text: Soak the gelatine leaves in a bowl of cold water for 5 minutes until soft and floppy.
Pour the cream, milk, and sugar into a saucepan. Add the vanilla. Warm over a low heat, stirring, until the sugar dissolves.
Remove from the heat before it boils. Squeeze the water from the gelatine leaves and add them to the warm cream.
Stir until the gelatine is fully dissolved. Strain through a fine sieve into a jug.
Pour into lightly oiled ramekins or glasses. Leave to cool, then refrigerate for at least 4 hours.
To unmould, run a knife around the edge and invert onto a plate. Or serve in the glass with fruit sauce poured over.

items.symptom: The panna cotta did not set
items.cause: Not enough gelatine, or the gelatine did not fully dissolve before chilling.
items.fix: Next time ensure all the gelatine dissolves in the warm cream. If it has not set after 6 hours, return it to a saucepan, melt, add another half-leaf of soaked gelatine, and re-set.

items.symptom: The texture is rubbery rather than silky
items.fix: Three leaves for 600ml total liquid is correct. More gives a bouncy set rather than a trembling one.

items.symptom: The panna cotta will not come out of the mould
items.cause: The ramekin was not oiled, or it was not loosened around the edge.
items.fix: Oil the ramekins lightly with a neutral oil before filling. Run a thin knife around the edge before inverting. Serve in the glass if unmoulding is not working.

content.text: Panna cotta is a Piedmontese dessert, made in the rich dairy country around Langhe and Monferrato. It appears on restaurant menus across Italy as a light finish to a big meal. The combination with sharp berries or caramel is classic. It is one of the easiest restaurant-quality desserts a home cook can make.
